oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: More productive and competitive business ecosystem designed to improve people's standards of living and well-being
oc.description: Outcome 1: The small size of Caribbean economies and the shortfalls in innovation and digital transformation influence the level of productivity and overall competitiveness of the region. Achieving sustainable transformation of the Caribbean business environment requires the enhanced productivity of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises’ (MSMEs), which can only be achieved by creating a more productive and competitive business ecosystem. Involving  the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership. Involving the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership.  An important element to this area is the establishment of innovative and sustainable financial architecture that can enable MSME access to financial markets. The United Nations can play an important interlocuter role between private-sector financiers, the public sector and other (international) financial institutions.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: National governments and regional institutions use relevant data to design and adopt laws and policies to eliminate discrimination, address structural inequalities and ensure the advancement of those left furthest behind
oc.description: In order to reduce inequalities and enhance people’s health and well-being, legislative and policy frameworks should eliminate discrimination, support equality, address the social and environmental determinants of health, provide for universal coverage and access to quality social and health services and help those furthest behind to claim their rights, ensuring they are not left behind.  Strengthened capabilities for data collection and analysis, including on application of the principles of a human rights-based approach to data and indicators (HRBAD) , and strong and harmonized data collection system are required.  These will support evidence-based policy and planning processes that should employ rights-based and gender-responsive approaches and an attention to the multidimensional nature of vulnerabilities.

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: People in the Caribbean equitably access and utilize universal, quality and shock-responsive, social protection, education, health, and care services
oc.description: Outcome 4 specifically aims at improving quality, coverage and access to health, education, housing, social protection, and care services, as well as the benefits (good health, learning, dignity, and decent living standards) that these services aim to deliver.  Access to quality services that are shock- and gender-responsive is an important mechanism for income redistribution, helping to tackle the underlying causes of extreme poverty and persistent inequality which have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean people, communities, and institutions enhance their adaptive capacity for inclusive, gender responsive DRM and climate change adaptation and mitigation
oc.description: Safeguarding pre-crisis development gains and strengthening the resilience of countries that are both directly and indirectly affected by natural, socio-natural, and anthropogenic hazards are key concepts within this outcome area. This means reducing the existing vulnerabilities (including its drivers) and exposure; increasing capacities; and minimizing the need for external support in responding to emergencies, notwithstanding the focus on regional cooperation for response and recovery.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: Regional and national laws, policies, systems, and institutions improve access to justice and promote peace, social cohesion, and security
oc.description: Citizen security and social cohesion in the Caribbean region is threatened by high levels of crime and violence, including gender-based violence, fueled by social inequalities that interact with illicit external flows, like the trafficking in drugs and weapons, and by corruption.  To ensure that societies are safe, fair, and cohesive, it is necessary that an enabling environment is created, and duty bearers are mobilized to effect change.

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
oc.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: People in the Caribbean and communities actively contribute to and benefit from building and maintaining safer, fairer, more inclusive, and equitable societies
oc.description: The Caribbean struggles with high rates of crime, inequality and inequity that adversely impacts the lives and realities of people living the Caribbean. Personal safety and security are threatened both by violence in the home and in the community and impacts the ability of people to live full and productive lives. It is crucial to tackle the root causes that hinder the creation of safe, fair, inclusive, and equitable societies and which promote and perpetuate violence and insecurity.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: More productive and competitive business ecosystem designed to improve people's standards of living and well-being
oc.description: Outcome 1: The small size of Caribbean economies and the shortfalls in innovation and digital transformation influence the level of productivity and overall competitiveness of the region. Achieving sustainable transformation of the Caribbean business environment requires the enhanced productivity of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises’ (MSMEs), which can only be achieved by creating a more productive and competitive business ecosystem. Involving  the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership. Involving the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership.  An important element to this area is the establishment of innovative and sustainable financial architecture that can enable MSME access to financial markets. The United Nations can play an important interlocuter role between private-sector financiers, the public sector and other (international) financial institutions.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: The Caribbean has fully transitioned to a more diversified and sustainable economy that supports inclusive and resilient economic growth

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: National governments and regional institutions use relevant data to design and adopt laws and policies to eliminate discrimination, address structural inequalities and ensure the advancement of those left furthest behind
oc.description: In order to reduce inequalities and enhance people’s health and well-being, legislative and policy frameworks should eliminate discrimination, support equality, address the social and environmental determinants of health, provide for universal coverage and access to quality social and health services and help those furthest behind to claim their rights, ensuring they are not left behind.  Strengthened capabilities for data collection and analysis, including on application of the principles of a human rights-based approach to data and indicators (HRBAD) , and strong and harmonized data collection system are required.  These will support evidence-based policy and planning processes that should employ rights-based and gender-responsive approaches and an attention to the multidimensional nature of vulnerabilities.

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: People in the Caribbean equitably access and utilize universal, quality and shock-responsive, social protection, education, health, and care services
oc.description: Outcome 4 specifically aims at improving quality, coverage and access to health, education, housing, social protection, and care services, as well as the benefits (good health, learning, dignity, and decent living standards) that these services aim to deliver.  Access to quality services that are shock- and gender-responsive is an important mechanism for income redistribution, helping to tackle the underlying causes of extreme poverty and persistent inequality which have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean people, communities, and institutions enhance their adaptive capacity for inclusive, gender responsive DRM and climate change adaptation and mitigation
oc.description: Safeguarding pre-crisis development gains and strengthening the resilience of countries that are both directly and indirectly affected by natural, socio-natural, and anthropogenic hazards are key concepts within this outcome area. This means reducing the existing vulnerabilities (including its drivers) and exposure; increasing capacities; and minimizing the need for external support in responding to emergencies, notwithstanding the focus on regional cooperation for response and recovery.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: Regional and national laws, policies, systems, and institutions improve access to justice and promote peace, social cohesion, and security
oc.description: Citizen security and social cohesion in the Caribbean region is threatened by high levels of crime and violence, including gender-based violence, fueled by social inequalities that interact with illicit external flows, like the trafficking in drugs and weapons, and by corruption.  To ensure that societies are safe, fair, and cohesive, it is necessary that an enabling environment is created, and duty bearers are mobilized to effect change.

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
oc.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: People in the Caribbean and communities actively contribute to and benefit from building and maintaining safer, fairer, more inclusive, and equitable societies
oc.description: The Caribbean struggles with high rates of crime, inequality and inequity that adversely impacts the lives and realities of people living the Caribbean. Personal safety and security are threatened both by violence in the home and in the community and impacts the ability of people to live full and productive lives. It is crucial to tackle the root causes that hinder the creation of safe, fair, inclusive, and equitable societies and which promote and perpetuate violence and insecurity.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: More productive and competitive business ecosystem designed to improve people's standards of living and well-being
oc.description: Outcome 1: The small size of Caribbean economies and the shortfalls in innovation and digital transformation influence the level of productivity and overall competitiveness of the region. Achieving sustainable transformation of the Caribbean business environment requires the enhanced productivity of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises’ (MSMEs), which can only be achieved by creating a more productive and competitive business ecosystem. Involving  the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership. Involving the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership.  An important element to this area is the establishment of innovative and sustainable financial architecture that can enable MSME access to financial markets. The United Nations can play an important interlocuter role between private-sector financiers, the public sector and other (international) financial institutions.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: The Caribbean has fully transitioned to a more diversified and sustainable economy that supports inclusive and resilient economic growth

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: National governments and regional institutions use relevant data to design and adopt laws and policies to eliminate discrimination, address structural inequalities and ensure the advancement of those left furthest behind
oc.description: In order to reduce inequalities and enhance people’s health and well-being, legislative and policy frameworks should eliminate discrimination, support equality, address the social and environmental determinants of health, provide for universal coverage and access to quality social and health services and help those furthest behind to claim their rights, ensuring they are not left behind.  Strengthened capabilities for data collection and analysis, including on application of the principles of a human rights-based approach to data and indicators (HRBAD) , and strong and harmonized data collection system are required.  These will support evidence-based policy and planning processes that should employ rights-based and gender-responsive approaches and an attention to the multidimensional nature of vulnerabilities.

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: People in the Caribbean equitably access and utilize universal, quality and shock-responsive, social protection, education, health, and care services
oc.description: Outcome 4 specifically aims at improving quality, coverage and access to health, education, housing, social protection, and care services, as well as the benefits (good health, learning, dignity, and decent living standards) that these services aim to deliver.  Access to quality services that are shock- and gender-responsive is an important mechanism for income redistribution, helping to tackle the underlying causes of extreme poverty and persistent inequality which have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean people, communities, and institutions enhance their adaptive capacity for inclusive, gender responsive DRM and climate change adaptation and mitigation
oc.description: Safeguarding pre-crisis development gains and strengthening the resilience of countries that are both directly and indirectly affected by natural, socio-natural, and anthropogenic hazards are key concepts within this outcome area. This means reducing the existing vulnerabilities (including its drivers) and exposure; increasing capacities; and minimizing the need for external support in responding to emergencies, notwithstanding the focus on regional cooperation for response and recovery.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: Regional and national laws, policies, systems, and institutions improve access to justice and promote peace, social cohesion, and security
oc.description: Citizen security and social cohesion in the Caribbean region is threatened by high levels of crime and violence, including gender-based violence, fueled by social inequalities that interact with illicit external flows, like the trafficking in drugs and weapons, and by corruption.  To ensure that societies are safe, fair, and cohesive, it is necessary that an enabling environment is created, and duty bearers are mobilized to effect change.

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
oc.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: People in the Caribbean and communities actively contribute to and benefit from building and maintaining safer, fairer, more inclusive, and equitable societies
oc.description: The Caribbean struggles with high rates of crime, inequality and inequity that adversely impacts the lives and realities of people living the Caribbean. Personal safety and security are threatened both by violence in the home and in the community and impacts the ability of people to live full and productive lives. It is crucial to tackle the root causes that hinder the creation of safe, fair, inclusive, and equitable societies and which promote and perpetuate violence and insecurity.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: More productive and competitive business ecosystem designed to improve people's standards of living and well-being
oc.description: Outcome 1: The small size of Caribbean economies and the shortfalls in innovation and digital transformation influence the level of productivity and overall competitiveness of the region. Achieving sustainable transformation of the Caribbean business environment requires the enhanced productivity of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises’ (MSMEs), which can only be achieved by creating a more productive and competitive business ecosystem. Involving  the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership. Involving the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership.  An important element to this area is the establishment of innovative and sustainable financial architecture that can enable MSME access to financial markets. The United Nations can play an important interlocuter role between private-sector financiers, the public sector and other (international) financial institutions.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: The Caribbean has fully transitioned to a more diversified and sustainable economy that supports inclusive and resilient economic growth

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: National governments and regional institutions use relevant data to design and adopt laws and policies to eliminate discrimination, address structural inequalities and ensure the advancement of those left furthest behind
oc.description: In order to reduce inequalities and enhance people’s health and well-being, legislative and policy frameworks should eliminate discrimination, support equality, address the social and environmental determinants of health, provide for universal coverage and access to quality social and health services and help those furthest behind to claim their rights, ensuring they are not left behind.  Strengthened capabilities for data collection and analysis, including on application of the principles of a human rights-based approach to data and indicators (HRBAD) , and strong and harmonized data collection system are required.  These will support evidence-based policy and planning processes that should employ rights-based and gender-responsive approaches and an attention to the multidimensional nature of vulnerabilities.

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: People in the Caribbean equitably access and utilize universal, quality and shock-responsive, social protection, education, health, and care services
oc.description: Outcome 4 specifically aims at improving quality, coverage and access to health, education, housing, social protection, and care services, as well as the benefits (good health, learning, dignity, and decent living standards) that these services aim to deliver.  Access to quality services that are shock- and gender-responsive is an important mechanism for income redistribution, helping to tackle the underlying causes of extreme poverty and persistent inequality which have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean people, communities, and institutions enhance their adaptive capacity for inclusive, gender responsive DRM and climate change adaptation and mitigation
oc.description: Safeguarding pre-crisis development gains and strengthening the resilience of countries that are both directly and indirectly affected by natural, socio-natural, and anthropogenic hazards are key concepts within this outcome area. This means reducing the existing vulnerabilities (including its drivers) and exposure; increasing capacities; and minimizing the need for external support in responding to emergencies, notwithstanding the focus on regional cooperation for response and recovery.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: Regional and national laws, policies, systems, and institutions improve access to justice and promote peace, social cohesion, and security
oc.description: Citizen security and social cohesion in the Caribbean region is threatened by high levels of crime and violence, including gender-based violence, fueled by social inequalities that interact with illicit external flows, like the trafficking in drugs and weapons, and by corruption.  To ensure that societies are safe, fair, and cohesive, it is necessary that an enabling environment is created, and duty bearers are mobilized to effect change.

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
oc.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: People in the Caribbean and communities actively contribute to and benefit from building and maintaining safer, fairer, more inclusive, and equitable societies
oc.description: The Caribbean struggles with high rates of crime, inequality and inequity that adversely impacts the lives and realities of people living the Caribbean. Personal safety and security are threatened both by violence in the home and in the community and impacts the ability of people to live full and productive lives. It is crucial to tackle the root causes that hinder the creation of safe, fair, inclusive, and equitable societies and which promote and perpetuate violence and insecurity.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: More productive and competitive business ecosystem designed to improve people's standards of living and well-being
oc.description: Outcome 1: The small size of Caribbean economies and the shortfalls in innovation and digital transformation influence the level of productivity and overall competitiveness of the region. Achieving sustainable transformation of the Caribbean business environment requires the enhanced productivity of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises’ (MSMEs), which can only be achieved by creating a more productive and competitive business ecosystem. Involving  the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership. Involving the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership.  An important element to this area is the establishment of innovative and sustainable financial architecture that can enable MSME access to financial markets. The United Nations can play an important interlocuter role between private-sector financiers, the public sector and other (international) financial institutions.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: The Caribbean has fully transitioned to a more diversified and sustainable economy that supports inclusive and resilient economic growth

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: National governments and regional institutions use relevant data to design and adopt laws and policies to eliminate discrimination, address structural inequalities and ensure the advancement of those left furthest behind
oc.description: In order to reduce inequalities and enhance people’s health and well-being, legislative and policy frameworks should eliminate discrimination, support equality, address the social and environmental determinants of health, provide for universal coverage and access to quality social and health services and help those furthest behind to claim their rights, ensuring they are not left behind.  Strengthened capabilities for data collection and analysis, including on application of the principles of a human rights-based approach to data and indicators (HRBAD) , and strong and harmonized data collection system are required.  These will support evidence-based policy and planning processes that should employ rights-based and gender-responsive approaches and an attention to the multidimensional nature of vulnerabilities.

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: People in the Caribbean equitably access and utilize universal, quality and shock-responsive, social protection, education, health, and care services
oc.description: Outcome 4 specifically aims at improving quality, coverage and access to health, education, housing, social protection, and care services, as well as the benefits (good health, learning, dignity, and decent living standards) that these services aim to deliver.  Access to quality services that are shock- and gender-responsive is an important mechanism for income redistribution, helping to tackle the underlying causes of extreme poverty and persistent inequality which have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean people, communities, and institutions enhance their adaptive capacity for inclusive, gender responsive DRM and climate change adaptation and mitigation
oc.description: Safeguarding pre-crisis development gains and strengthening the resilience of countries that are both directly and indirectly affected by natural, socio-natural, and anthropogenic hazards are key concepts within this outcome area. This means reducing the existing vulnerabilities (including its drivers) and exposure; increasing capacities; and minimizing the need for external support in responding to emergencies, notwithstanding the focus on regional cooperation for response and recovery.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: Regional and national laws, policies, systems, and institutions improve access to justice and promote peace, social cohesion, and security
oc.description: Citizen security and social cohesion in the Caribbean region is threatened by high levels of crime and violence, including gender-based violence, fueled by social inequalities that interact with illicit external flows, like the trafficking in drugs and weapons, and by corruption.  To ensure that societies are safe, fair, and cohesive, it is necessary that an enabling environment is created, and duty bearers are mobilized to effect change.

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
oc.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: People in the Caribbean and communities actively contribute to and benefit from building and maintaining safer, fairer, more inclusive, and equitable societies
oc.description: The Caribbean struggles with high rates of crime, inequality and inequity that adversely impacts the lives and realities of people living the Caribbean. Personal safety and security are threatened both by violence in the home and in the community and impacts the ability of people to live full and productive lives. It is crucial to tackle the root causes that hinder the creation of safe, fair, inclusive, and equitable societies and which promote and perpetuate violence and insecurity.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: More productive and competitive business ecosystem designed to improve people's standards of living and well-being
oc.description: Outcome 1: The small size of Caribbean economies and the shortfalls in innovation and digital transformation influence the level of productivity and overall competitiveness of the region. Achieving sustainable transformation of the Caribbean business environment requires the enhanced productivity of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises’ (MSMEs), which can only be achieved by creating a more productive and competitive business ecosystem. Involving  the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership. Involving the private sector  early on in the transformation process is  essential given its  increasingly important role in achieving inclusive sustainable development, including through public-private partnership.  An important element to this area is the establishment of innovative and sustainable financial architecture that can enable MSME access to financial markets. The United Nations can play an important interlocuter role between private-sector financiers, the public sector and other (international) financial institutions.

oc.parentName: Economic resilience and Shared prosperity
oc.name: The Caribbean has fully transitioned to a more diversified and sustainable economy that supports inclusive and resilient economic growth

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: National governments and regional institutions use relevant data to design and adopt laws and policies to eliminate discrimination, address structural inequalities and ensure the advancement of those left furthest behind
oc.description: In order to reduce inequalities and enhance people’s health and well-being, legislative and policy frameworks should eliminate discrimination, support equality, address the social and environmental determinants of health, provide for universal coverage and access to quality social and health services and help those furthest behind to claim their rights, ensuring they are not left behind.  Strengthened capabilities for data collection and analysis, including on application of the principles of a human rights-based approach to data and indicators (HRBAD) , and strong and harmonized data collection system are required.  These will support evidence-based policy and planning processes that should employ rights-based and gender-responsive approaches and an attention to the multidimensional nature of vulnerabilities.

oc.parentName: Equality, Well-Being and Leaving No One Behind
oc.name: People in the Caribbean equitably access and utilize universal, quality and shock-responsive, social protection, education, health, and care services
oc.description: Outcome 4 specifically aims at improving quality, coverage and access to health, education, housing, social protection, and care services, as well as the benefits (good health, learning, dignity, and decent living standards) that these services aim to deliver.  Access to quality services that are shock- and gender-responsive is an important mechanism for income redistribution, helping to tackle the underlying causes of extreme poverty and persistent inequality which have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean people, communities, and institutions enhance their adaptive capacity for inclusive, gender responsive DRM and climate change adaptation and mitigation
oc.description: Safeguarding pre-crisis development gains and strengthening the resilience of countries that are both directly and indirectly affected by natural, socio-natural, and anthropogenic hazards are key concepts within this outcome area. This means reducing the existing vulnerabilities (including its drivers) and exposure; increasing capacities; and minimizing the need for external support in responding to emergencies, notwithstanding the focus on regional cooperation for response and recovery.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: Regional and national laws, policies, systems, and institutions improve access to justice and promote peace, social cohesion, and security
oc.description: Citizen security and social cohesion in the Caribbean region is threatened by high levels of crime and violence, including gender-based violence, fueled by social inequalities that interact with illicit external flows, like the trafficking in drugs and weapons, and by corruption.  To ensure that societies are safe, fair, and cohesive, it is necessary that an enabling environment is created, and duty bearers are mobilized to effect change.

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
oc.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: People in the Caribbean and communities actively contribute to and benefit from building and maintaining safer, fairer, more inclusive, and equitable societies
oc.description: The Caribbean struggles with high rates of crime, inequality and inequity that adversely impacts the lives and realities of people living the Caribbean. Personal safety and security are threatened both by violence in the home and in the community and impacts the ability of people to live full and productive lives. It is crucial to tackle the root causes that hinder the creation of safe, fair, inclusive, and equitable societies and which promote and perpetuate violence and insecurity.

oc.name: Caribbean people, communities, and institutions enhance their adaptive capacity for inclusive, gender responsive DRM and climate change adaptation and mitigation
oc.description: Safeguarding pre-crisis development gains and strengthening the resilience of countries that are both directly and indirectly affected by natural, socio-natural, and anthropogenic hazards are key concepts within this outcome area. This means reducing the existing vulnerabilities (including its drivers) and exposure; increasing capacities; and minimizing the need for external support in responding to emergencies, notwithstanding the focus on regional cooperation for response and recovery.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: Regional and national laws, policies, systems, and institutions improve access to justice and promote peace, social cohesion, and security
oc.description: Citizen security and social cohesion in the Caribbean region is threatened by high levels of crime and violence, including gender-based violence, fueled by social inequalities that interact with illicit external flows, like the trafficking in drugs and weapons, and by corruption.  To ensure that societies are safe, fair, and cohesive, it is necessary that an enabling environment is created, and duty bearers are mobilized to effect change.

oc.parentName: Resilience to Climate Change and Sustainable Natural Resource Management
oc.name: Caribbean countries manage natural resources and ecosystems to strengthen their resilience and enhance the resilience and prosperity of the people and communities that depend on them.
oc.description: Caribbean economies are highly dependent on the region’s natural resources and biodiverse ecosystems, both of which provide key services and co-benefits to people and communities. Economic resilience is, however, a critical challenge for the region in the face of environmental, climate and disaster risks, which collectively destroy natural resources and limit the region’s transformative capacity. The challenges of desertification, forest management, biodiversity loss and climate change are interrelated and need to be collectively addressed to achieve sustainable development in the Caribbean.  Both marine and terrestrial biodiversity conservation are acute issues requiring prioritization to ensure the sustainable use of ecosystems. Nature-based solutions that tackle overexploitation and address pollution and waste management should be optimised with specific attention provided to food and water security, a challenge that was further evidenced during the COVID-19 crisis.

oc.parentName: Peace, Safety, Justice, and the Rule of Law
oc.name: People in the Caribbean and communities actively contribute to and benefit from building and maintaining safer, fairer, more inclusive, and equitable societies
oc.description: The Caribbean struggles with high rates of crime, inequality and inequity that adversely impacts the lives and realities of people living the Caribbean. Personal safety and security are threatened both by violence in the home and in the community and impacts the ability of people to live full and productive lives. It is crucial to tackle the root causes that hinder the creation of safe, fair, inclusive, and equitable societies and which promote and perpetuate violence and insecurity.

sp.name: Accès aux services sociaux de base et assistance humanitaire
sp.description: Celui -ci le troisème  axe de l'UNSDCF 2020-2024 à travers lequel le SNU contribuera   : i) à l’accès équitable, de qualité et durable surtout pour les populations les plus vulnérables et ii) à l’assistance des populations affectées par les situations d’urgence.

oc.parentName: Accès aux services sociaux de base et assistance humanitaire
oc.name: Les populations, en particulier les plus vulnérables bénéficient d’un accès équitable, de qualité et durable aux services sociaux de base, y compris de lutte contre le VIH/SIDA
oc.description:
Le SNU, qui inscrit ses appuis dans les principales cibles des ODD, mettra en œuvre un ensemble d’actions visant l’optimisation de ses appuis dans l’amélioration de l’accès à des services sociaux de base de qualité et efficaces, surtout pour les groupes les plus vulnérables, en particulier les femmes et les enfants. Les actions viseront le renforcement des capacités institutionnelles, techniques aux niveaux national, décentralisé et des communautés, le plaidoyer centré surtout sur les ODD, et l’offre de services sociaux de qualité et de façon durable. Un lien sera également réalisé avec la nécessité d’augmenter les opportunités de création de revenus des ménages afin de leur permettre d’accéder plus facilement aux services sociaux de base. 

Le SNU confortera et renforcera selon les zones géographiques et suivant les approches retenues, en particulier le Nexus « humanitaire, développement et paix », les initiatives d’accompagnement des partenaires nationaux (au niveau national, provincial et local) et d’autres partenaires pour la construction et la mise à niveau de certains centres de santé de base, d’infrastructures d’eau potable et d’assainissement. La composante des meilleures pratiques d’hygiène et nutritionnelles fera partie intégrante des appuis au niveau des écoles et à l’échelle communautaire.
 
Au niveau de l’éducation, le SNU mettra l’accent sur les cycles préscolaires, primaires et d’autres niveaux d’enseignement sur la base des objectifs sectoriels tout en prenant en considération plus particulièrement la scolarisation des filles et le système d’apprentissage alternatif existant y compris la formation professionnelle ; la question de mise à niveau des compétences des enseignants sera également partie intégrante des appuis envisagés. Dans ce cadre, le SNU contribuera aussi aux efforts d’alignement des politiques éducatives au regard des cibles ODD et à la mise en œuvre des programmes de diversification de l’offre éducative et d’amélioration de performances du secteur. 
  
Au niveau de la santé, le SNU mobilisera ses compétences et moyens pour renforcer les référentiels programmatiques du secteur de la santé et l’amélioration de la qualité des services intégrés y compris les interventions essentielles et d’urgence en matière de soins maternels et néonatals ainsi que la dotation d’équipements de chaîne d’approvisionnement fonctionnels. L’objectif est de contribuer efficacement à la réduction de la mortalité maternelle et néo natale à travers le renforcement des soins obstétricaux.  Les appuis viseront également à maintenir un bon niveau de couverture vaccinale chez la femme et l’enfant et à combattre la malnutrition chronique des enfants de moins de cinq ans. En matière de lutte contre le VIH/Sida, le SNU renforcera ses interventions de prévention, sur  les campagnes de sensibilisation et l’accès au traitement ARV et le suivi biologique en conformité avec l’objectif 90-90-90. Enfin, des actions visant la protection des femmes contre toutes les formes de violence seront entreprises dans le cadre du renforcement de l’autonomisation juridique, économique et sociale des femmes.

ou.name: Institutional capacities, mechanisms and policies enhanced to provide access to justice and protect human rights for all, especially those at risk of being left behind in compliance with international human rights standards.
ou.description:
Agencies: UNDP, UNODC, UNHCR, IOM, UNICEF																		
UNHCR through advocacy interventions and promotional events contributed to advance Institutional capacities. UNHCR  with the support of the partner and Ombudsperson Institution has organized high-level event with an aim to raise the awareness of the authorities on challenges and obstacles persons of concern face in addressing their requests for late birth registration, resulting with the authorities pledge to create a systemic mechanism for identification, prevention, reduction, and protection of unregistered persons at risk of statelessness. Extensive advocacies yield the results in authorities’ considerations for inclusion of the identified gaps and challenges into concept documents providing basis for the revision of laws for citizenship and civil status. 
Apart from daily advocacy interventions UNHCR has produced retorts and presented them in different events aiming at advancing the implementation and the protection of the rights of non-majority communities. UNHCR published a report “Sustainability and reintegration challenges of returnees/IDPs” at the high-level event with all relevant stakeholders that highlighted progress and challenges in various fields ranging from legislative/institutional developments, access to rights and services, housing, access to health services, education rights, child protection, security, and socio-economic integration. The reports produced and the improvements promoted relate to the implementation of the of the law on allocation for use and exchange of municipal immovable property was produced with special focus on returnees and IDP’s; implementation of the legal framework on social housing, specifically Law on Housing Financing Specific Programs; implementation of the Regulation No. 01/2018 for the return of displaced persons and durable solutions.
In addition UNHCR provided commentaries to 10 legal acts or strategies:  Namely, concept documents were produced for laws on citizenship, civil status, and residence, relating to persons at risk of statelessness and stateless persons. Contributions relating to IDPs and returnees were provided for the Draft Law on Population and Housing Census; Draft MCR Strategy for Protection and Promotion of the Rights of the Communities and their Members; Draft Strategy on Rule of Law with special focus on access to rights, socio-economic integration, property issues and court proceedings; draft Law on Early Education for children of 0-6 years; draft amended Law on Free legal Aid; and draft Law on Local Self-Government.

UN-Habitat: UN-Habitat has been supporting the municipalities in Mitrovica Region in increasing environmental performance and climate responsiveness through spatial planning documents and their respective Strategic Environmental Assessments (SEAs), as well as Sustainable Urban Mobility Plans (SUMPs). SEAs provide analysis on environmental sustainability in spatial plans (including analysis on pollution levels, habitats of endangered species, flood zone susceptibility, land degradation, etc.) aiming to improve environmental protection, human health and quality of life, while reducing negative impacts of the measures foreseen in the respective plans and promoting sustainable development. Whereas SUMPs are sectorial plans designed to tackle transport-related problems in urban areas more efficiently and sustainably, which aim to improve and harmonize the needs of all traffic participants for free and safe movement within a functional urban area while enhancing living comfort, ensuring a better quality of life, and at the same time reducing transport-related emissions.

ou.name: Strengthening institutional capacities of ministry responsible for environment, MAFRD and municipal authorities to plan for integrated, gender responsive, sustainable, and inclusive management of land and forestry resources
ou.description:
Agencies: UN Habitat; FAO			

UN-Habitat: UN-Habitat has been supporting 7 municipalities in Mitrovica Region (including Mitrovica South, Mitrovica North, Vushtrri/Vucitrn and Skenderaj/Srbica, Zubin Potok, Zvecan and Leposavic) to develop integrated and participatory spatial planning documents, including Municipal Development Plans (MDPs) and Municipal Zoning Maps (MZMs). MDP is a multi-sectoral document that defines the long-term limits of economic, social and spatial development, whereas MZM determines in detail (through graphs, photos, maps and text) the type, destination, planned spatial use and action measures that are based on the duration and justifiable projections for public and private investment for all the territory of the municipality. COVID-19 lock down measures provided challenges for organizing meetings with municipal counterparts, citizens and other stakeholders regarding public consultations in Mitrovica Region, whereas local elections and related activities prolonged the approval of strategic development documents. Not all Municipal Planning Team members were trained and technically equipped to work remotely. Additional challenges remain in obtaining adequate data from institutions functioning in the Serbian system.

sp.description: En 2025 el país habrá impulsado un modelo de desarrollo económico sostenible e inclusivo, fomentado la productividad con mayor valor agregado, así como las exportaciones, la diversificación de la matriz productiva, la innovación y la incorporación de ciencia y tecnología, para generar trabajo decente, sostenible y productivo, y para reducir las cantidad de personas en situación de pobreza multidimensional, las desigualdades de género y las vulnerabilidades a nivel territorial, sin dejar a nadie atrás.

sp.name: Desarrollo Social
sp.description: En 2025 el país habrá fortalecido y profundizado las capacidades del Estado para garantizar los derechos de todas las personas, con especial atención a aquellas en mayores condiciones de vulnerabilidad. Se apoyará el desarrollo de políticas basadas en evidencia, con enfoque de derechos y perspectiva de género, la asignación de presupuestos suficientes y sostenibles, la ampliación de la oferta de servicios incluyentes y de calidad, y la promoción de la capacidad de agencia de las personas para ejercer y demandar la garantía de sus derechos

sp.name: Sostenibilidad Ambiental
sp.description: En 2025 el país habrá logrado una transición justa hacia una economía verde. Promoverá la protección ambiental, la resiliencia y las acciones de mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático. Instalará y profundizará el enfoque ambiental en la gestión y el impulso de políticas públicas, y promoverá cambios de comportamiento en actores clave del desarrollo sostenible, con perspectiva de género y derechos humanos.

sp.name: Gobernanza
sp.description: En 2025 el país habrá mejorado la gobernanza inclusiva, la eficiencia y la eficacia de la gestión pública mediante la articulación interinstitucional, intergubernamental e interjurisdiccional y la cooperación multilateral. A la vez, habrá mejorado en el cumplimiento de las normativas internacionales de derechos humanos y género, y habrá fortalecido los mecanismos de participación de todas las poblaciones, en especial aquellas en mayores condiciones de vulnerabilidad, incorporando perspectiva de género e interseccionalidad.

sp.name: Strategic Priority 1: Inclusive and Sustainable Economic Development
sp.description: Focusing on economic transformation – pursuing an accelerated shift towards more sustainable and inclusive economic growth, with increased and equitable opportunities for decent jobs and livelihoods.

sp.name: Strategic Priority 2: Equitable Human Development and Well Being
sp.description:
Encompassing human capabilities and social development, addressing gaps in health, nutrition, food security, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), education and learning, child and youth protection,
migration services, and social protection.

sp.name: Strategic Priority 3: Sustainable, Healthy and Resilient Environment
sp.description:
Focusing on Bangladesh accelerating actions on climate change resilience and adaptation; natural resources and water management; renewable energy and a transition to environmental sustainability,
along with reducing vulnerabilities to natural hazards.

sp.name: Strategic Priority 4: Transformative, Participatory and Inclusive Governance
sp.description: Aiming to ensure more inclusive, gender-responsive and accountable governance systems and that all people are empowered, engaged, and enjoy all human rights, peace, non-violence, justice, and security.

sp.name: Strategic Priority 5: Gender Equality and Eliminating Gender-Based Violence
sp.description: This cross-cutting Strategic Priority addresses structural and intersectoral gender inequalities and gender-based violence to foster an environment in which women, girls and sexual minorities live free from discrimination and violence.

oc.parentName: Strategic Priority 1: Inclusive and Sustainable Economic Development
oc.name: Outcome 1: By 2026 people, more people in Bangladesh, particularly the most vulnerable and marginalized from all gender and social groups and those from lagging districts benefit from sustainable livelihood and decent work opportunities resulting from responsible, inclusive, sustainable, green and equitable economic development.
oc.description:
To achieve the stated Outcome at least three sets of conditions must be fulfilled. 
First, Bangladesh will need to deploy and adopt SDG financing frameworks and whole-of-society approaches including the Integrated National Financing Framework (INFF) to leverage partnerships and multiple sources of finance to increase investments in diversified, employment-intensive, gender-transformative, sustainable, and responsible green growth sectors and resilient infrastructure, promoting equitable and inclusive employment.

Second, people in Bangladesh and migrant workers working abroad, especially young women and men from vulnerable and marginalised communities, must have market-driven skills development, and access to financial and non-financial services that enable them to benefit from inclusive national and global employment, and green entrepreneurship opportunities in the context of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

Third, Bangladesh must have strengthened institutions and governance frameworks for the labour market that drive formalisation of enterprises, responsible business practices, and that promote and protect dignity, rights, safety, and equity and equality at work, regardless of gender, disability, social and economic backgrounds and other identities including migrant status. and entrepreneurship opportunities mainly for youth, women and the most vulnerable and
marginalized communities.

oc.parentName: Strategic Priority 2: Equitable Human Development and Well Being
oc.name: Outcome 2: By 2026, more people, in particular, the most vulnerable and marginalized, have improved access to and utilization of quality, inclusive, gender- and shock-responsive, universal, and resilient social protection, social safety-net and basic social services.

oc.parentName: Strategic Priority 3: Sustainable, Healthy and Resilient Environment
oc.name: Outcome 3: By 2026, ecosystems are healthier, and all people, in particular the most vulnerable and marginalized in both rural and urban settings, benefit from and contribute in a gender-responsive manner to a cleaner and more resilient environment, an enriched natural resource base, low carbon development, and are prosperous and more resilient to climate change, shocks and disasters.

oc.parentName: Strategic Priority 4: Transformative, Participatory and Inclusive Governance
oc.name: Outcome 4: By 2026, more people, especially the most vulnerable, benefit from more equitable, nondiscriminatory, gender-responsive, participatory, accountable governance and justice, in a peaceful and tolerant society governed by the rule of law.

oc.parentName: Strategic Priority 5: Gender Equality and Eliminating Gender-Based Violence
oc.name: Outcome 5: By 2026, more women, girls and sexual minorities benefit from an environment in which they are empowered to exercise their rights, agency and decision-making power over all aspects of their lives and towards a life free from all forms of discrimination, violence and harmful norms and practices.

ou.name: E2: Subgrupo Desarrollo Industrial - Resultado 1 : Mejorar la productividad, generación de ingresos y capacidad de acceso a mercados de unidades productivas, con enfoque de inclusión social
ou.description:
La visión del subgrupo es ayudar al Estado Plurinacional de Bolivia a acelerar su transformación hacia una industrialización inclusiva y sostenible con oportunidades de empleo digno y trabajo decente hacia la recuperación socioeconómica, aprovechando las oportunidades de desarrollo industrial sostenible para lograr la Agenda 2030 y los ODS. Más que nunca, dado que la primera prioridad definida por el Gobierno es la reactivación económica, abrir caminos inclusivos y sostenibles con trabajo decente hacia el desarrollo industrial requiere enfoques sistémicos e integrales. El impacto de la industria se produce en sistemas cada vez más complejos, influenciados por las tendencias globales, la gobernanza multinivel y los avances tecnológicos exponenciales, con una gran variedad de partes interesadas involucradas en horizontes a más largo plazo. Asimismo, ese desarrollo industrial debe apuntar a cumplir con la Agenda 2030, favoreciendo el principio de "No Dejar a Nadie Atrás". En este sentido, se requiere enfocar las acciones en promoción de oportunidades de empleos formales y las condiciones de trabajo decente, en cumplimiento de la normativa laboral internacional y nacional vigentes. Al mismo tiempo, se debe trabajar en prevee reforzar las intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a mercados con productos / servicios de valor agregado.  

Para asegurar que la industrialización beneficie a todas y todos, permitiendo el acceso a los insumos y productos de fabricación y los dividendos industriales, se requiere que los esfuerzos sean concertados entre los actores públicos, privados y la sociedad civil, para garantizar  el desarrollo industrial sea sostenible, inclusivo y justo, con el fin de que las empresas puedan desarrollarse y que las personas puedan acceder a los nuevos empleos, con habilidades actualizadas, en condiciones de trabajo decente y alineadas a los requerimientos de los mercados laborales; en este marco, es importante señalar que los resultados y programas se deben constituir, también, en la agenda pública.

-El desarrollo industrial inclusivo y sostenible con trabajo decente, es considerado una estratégia esencial hacia una recuperación socioeconómica justa y equitativa, con un enfoque anclado en el territorio a fin de reforzar la continuidad de apoyos urbano - rural. 

Este contexto plantea el desafío de trabajar en tres niveles de forma coordinada y amplia:
i) Macro: Apoyo al desarrollo de Políticas y Normas Nacionales para la recuperación socio-económica del sector productivo incluyendo sectores estratégicos y/o emergentes, que contribuyen a la reactivación socioeconómica integral. 
ii) Meso:  Desarrollo de Programas y Proyectos a nivel subnacional con enfoque de promoción de la industrialización con oportunidades de empleo, con enfoque intersectorial que aborden a poblaciones en situación de mayor vulnerabilidad. 
iii) Micro: Desarrollo de Acciones Piloto con productores/as y unidades económicas  a nivel urbano y rural, incluyendo asociaciones de pequeños/as agricultores/as, cooperativas y MIPYME.

oc.description:
1) Programa Tu Oportunidad: During 2022, SCE Chile launched a new evidence-based methodology (based on the results of a previously developed pilot program), with two learning routes, one towards entrepreneurship and the other towards employability, depending to the participant’s profile (beginner/advanced). This methodology was implemented by the AIEP, a renown technical education institute, that undertook the mission to address the economic empowerment of women, migrants, and indigenous people with socioeconomic vulnerability through a sustainable model for technical education in this area. In addition, this institution is leveraging its vast network of private and public actors to increase opportunities for participants through referrals to entrepreneurship and employment clusters. As part of its sustainability program its community of students and graduates are encouraged to engage in volunteering activities.  There are currently 6,476 women participating in this program and 1,660 have been mentored by the 140 volunteer mentors who belong to the Your Opportunity Mentor Network. Another 542 women have been trained to become mentors to other SCE women as well as agents of change in their communities.  In terms of impact, and according to the follow-up survey of graduates three and six months after graduating, 37% of women improved their income; 16% of women found employment; 20% returned to formal education; 24% started a new business; 36% improved the business they already had; and 44% continued their education, all thanks to the AIEP program.
The AIEP program also strengthened its regional and national partnerships, identifying opportunities for collaborative projects and establishing labor reference protocols with the Ministry of the Interior, local governments and civil society organizations. Specifically in the northern region of the country, partnerships for the implementation of programmes and linkages have been strengthened (including SERNAMEG - National Women's Service, and SECREDUC - Regional Education Agency). More importantly, SCE Chile has been actively involved in the IOM/UNHCR-led roundtable on migration. In the southern zone, alliances have been developed in the Magallanes Region (including SERNAMEG, INDAP - National Institute of Agricultural Development, Venezuelans in Patagonia and other civil society institutions) to include more women from the most remote areas of the country. Simultaneously, SCE Chile has advanced in developing new partnerships with institutions and agencies for this new period of implementation (Ministry of Social Development,  INJUV, University of La Frontera and civil society).
In addition, SCE Chile led the public-private roundtable "More women in STEM education" which was developed jointly with Fundación País Digital (funded and supported by TELCOs and Technology companies in Chile) facilitating discussion among civil society actors, companies, universities and government to provide critical inputs and a gender approach for public policies in STEM education. Finally, SCE Chile prepared and disseminated a policy  report on Second Chance Education with a Gender Perspective with good practices and recommendations, contributing to public policy on online education and training for adult women.
2) Programa Originarias: During 2022, UN Women through its Originarias Programme contributed to the economic and social empowerment of more than 1,000 indigenous women in Chile, contributing towards the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals 1, 4, 5, 8, 12 and 17 of the 2030 Agenda and the strategic priorities of economic integration, education for work, citizen participation and effective exercise of human rights of the United Nations Cooperation Framework for Sustainable Development in Chile 2019-2022. 
Training and technical assistance provided by UN Women in conjunction with indigenous facilitators and academic and state institutions enabled more than 1,000 indigenous women to strengthen their leadership and advocacy skills, and more than 400 indigenous women entrepreneurs to access services, goods and resources, improving their opportunities for economic integration and participation in decision-making. 
The strategy implemented to actively train and promote the participation of indigenous trainers in intercultural learning spaces was a key factor for the success of the Originarias Program. The facilitators of the Originarias Program are mostly indigenous women (95%) who were trained in UN Women Training of Trainers schools. During 2012, these women, through the Originarias Program, participated in learning opportunities aimed at non-indigenous youth and adults and contributed to facilitate dialogues between indigenous women to elaborate proposals for economic development agendas. Finally, within the framework of the exercise of cultural rights, the program developed a school to improve the Aymara language skills of 28 intercultural educators, benefitting indirectly more than 4,000 indigenous children in the Tarapacá region.
As a result of the impacts generated by the Originarias Program, during 2022 a new donation agreement was signed with Teck Resources Ltd. for a total of 5.25 million dollars, which will enable the implementation of a 5-year process that will escalate over the years to incorporate new management strategies and financing mechanisms, to increasing the benefits  resulting from the Original Program and make these sustainable in the long term, placing the responsibility of strategic development on indigenous women themselves. With a proven methodology for empowerment, based on the integration of a rights, gender perspective and interculturality approach, the Originarias Program has the potential to be replicated in other territories, within Chile and in Latin America.
3) Proyecto Recuperación económica MPTF: Under the framework of the successful implementation of the MPTF program, UN Women during 2022 reached and established strategic alliances with many sectors of society (public, private, civil society, and communities), facilitating the  progress in different areas of gender equality, providing tools to improve women's economic opportunities, promoting leadership of micro-entrepreneur women, working with their businesses to include a gender perspective in their operation, raising awareness in the population in care co-responsibility issues, and generating information to guide the design of local and global policies.
One significant outcome of the program is related to the partnerships and collaboration networks that were created during its implementation and are still in place after the project's conclusion. The coordination of networks with different sectors and actors, the private and public sectors, employers and workers organizations, civil society, communities, and other initiatives from the UN, were crucial for creating better economic opportunities for women from the sectors most affected by the pandemic (heads of the household, migrants, women from rural areas, and caregivers). The MujeresEmplea.org virtual platform consolidated the offer of work and training opportunities, access to funds, and subsidies to entrepreneurship and care services (with more than 100 updated publications), with more than 67,000 visits during the implementation period. In parallel, the Activa Empresarias platform was created to connect the demand of products and services of large companies with the supply of companies led by women. 
A pilot training, mentoring, and community care services program was successfully designed and implemented. It positively impacted the insertion of women into the labor market. It allowed their economic activation mainly in three communes of Chile with high female social vulnerability rates (Renca, Padre las Casas, and San Pedro de Atacama). More than 9,000 women were trained in digital skills for employment and/or entrepreneurship, and more than 350 women were mentored for their labor insertion. The job fairs for women offered more than 33,000 job openings, to which more than 3,000 women applied. 
The childcare service was available in the selected territories to facilitate the access of their caregivers to training and work opportunities, providing care to 125 children per day.
A network of 300 women was trained and certified in care services, laying the foundations to establish a national caregiver's network, which the Government of Chile is currently promoting.
Awareness-raising and promoting care co-responsibility had a great reach among companies in the selected territories and the general population, promoting gender equality through communication plans and workshops designed for each target audience.

oc.description:
En el marco de la COP 25 bajo la presidencia de Chile, el país asumió el compromiso de profundizar en la agenda de género y la acción climática.  Para ello firmó acuerdo de colaboración con el Gran Ducado de Luxemburgo para implementar el proyecto “Género y cambio climático”, implementado por l Sistema de las Naciones Unidas y el Ministerio de Medio Ambiente.  En este proyecto, participaron el Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo (PNUD) y la Organización de las Naciones Unidas para la Alimentación y la Agricultura (FAO) y ONU Mujeres que lideró la ejecución del proyecto. El Éxito del proyecto, implicó que, en base a los resultados y lecciones aprendidas de esta iniciativa, que el Gran Ducado de Luxemburgo, decidiera apoyar por 4 años, a partir de 2023, una iniciativa regional, liderada por la Oficina Regional de ONU Mujeres, sobre cambio climático y enfoque de género. Los antecedentes y resultados del proyecto son los siguientes:

El objetivo principal del proyecto fue generar información que permita incorporar el enfoque de género en las políticas, programas y planes nacionales sectoriales de cambio climático. 

Para lograr el objetivo, se propuso generar información estadística e indicadores que den cuenta de las brechas de género existentes y permitan contar con datos desagregados para una mejor, eficiente y justa toma de decisiones, priorizando las áreas más urgente para reducir las desigualdades y el impacto medioambiental. Se crearon indicadores y un plan de monitoreo insertos en los planes nacionales de Adaptación y Mitigación, junto con programas específicos de género que considerearon el factor climático. Finalmente, la información obtenida fue puesta a disposición pública a través de la plataforma ARClim , visibilizando la distribución de las desigualdades por género, edad y territorio de la población desde el punto de vista climático.

En segundo lugar, al considerar la poca evidencia sobre la efectividad de programas existentes   en torno a género y cambio climático, el proyecto hizo hincapié en la importancia de incluir la perspectiva de género en las políticas sobre esta materia, dando a conocer y compartiendo avances sobre aquellas implementadas en el resto del mundo. 

En tercer lugar, el proyecto también propuso fortalecer las capacidades para una transversalización de género en temáticas ambientales, de funcionarios y funcionarias del Ministerio de Medio Ambiente, sociedad civil, academia y quienes toman decisiones a nivel nacional y regional. Ello, a través de capacitaciones, charlas y cursos especializados en Género y Medio Ambiente, con el fin de generar habilidades y conocimientos valiosos que ayuden a impulsar la inclusión de una perspectiva de género en las decisiones, programas y políticas medioambientales, así como también en el diálogo ciudadano. 

En relación a los avances, a nivel nacional se integró el enfoque de género en su Contribución Determinada a nivel Nacional (CDN), se presentó la Estrategia Climática de Largo Plazo (ECLP) con metas asociadas a la equidad e igualdad de género;  con el fin de generar conocimiento frente a los efectos diferenciados del cambio climático, se conformó una Mesa de Género y Cambio Climático de carácter intersectorial y se elaboraron cinco instrumentos además de integrar y complementar estas nuevas herramientas con otras iniciativas desarrolladas por el Ministerio de Medio Ambiente de Chile, en el país y la Región, como el Manual de Gestión para la Integración del enfoque de género en la acción climática, la Lista de Chequeo para integrar género en los instrumentos de cambio climático; y el estudio Generación de indicadores y análisis sectorial sobre género y cambio climático en cuatro sectores vulnerables al cambio climático: ciudades, pesca y acuicultura, biodiversidad y agricultura, modelo innovador y que servirá de base para apoyar a los distintos sectores que en el plazo de 2 años deben elaborar un plan de acción con enfoque de género en respuesta la reciente Ley Marco de Cambio climático.

ou.name: Actividades del  PLAN DE GESTIÓN DE ELIMINACIÓN DE HCFC (II)
ou.description:
En la 76ª Reunión del Comité Ejecutivo del Fondo Multilateral del Protocolo de Montreal se aprobaron fondos como parte de la Etapa II del Plan de Gestión de Eliminación de HCFC en Chile (HPMP-II) en Chile, para la implementación del componente de Servicios y Mantenimiento de el sector de la refrigeración y el aire acondicionado. Este componente es implementado por la Unidad Nacional de Ozono del Ministerio del Ambiente en coordinación con ONUDI.

En coordinación con el Gobierno de Chile, el sector industrial y ONUDI, se diseñó una estrategia para la eliminación de los HCFC utilizados en el sector de refrigeración y aire acondicionado, con el objetivo de ayudar al país a cumplir con las metas establecidas en el Protocolo de Montreal y por el Comité Ejecutivo del MP para 2020 y 2021, con base en las prioridades ya establecidas por el Gobierno para la Etapa II.

ou.name: Actividades del  PLAN DE GESTIÓN DE ELIMINACIÓN DE HCFC (III)
ou.description:
La Fase III del plan de gestión de eliminación de HCFC contiene cuatro líneas estratégicas, dentro de las cuales se encuentran la Línea Estratégica #2: “Programa de apoyo al sector de refrigeración y aire acondicionado” y la Línea Estratégica #4 “Programa de Monitoreo”, que incluyen las siguientes actividades:

1. Capacitación en mejores prácticas de refrigeración y aire acondicionado, y certificación de mujeres técnicas en habilidades RAC, para mejorar la gestión de HCFC y sus alternativas, reduciendo las emisiones al medio ambiente.
2. Asistencia técnica al sector RAC, a través del Programa Cero Fugas, para la realización de proyectos piloto en sistemas frigoríficos revisando y controlando sus fugas, consumo energético, consumos de refrigerante, para mejorar sus parámetros de rendimiento.
3. Asistencia técnica para los centros de recuperación, para mejorar su operación y capacidades de control de calidad para refrigerantes regenerados: y
4. Supervisión de la ejecución de las actividades del plan de gestión de eliminación de HCFC-III.
